claim: DYRK2 phosphorylates NDEL1 at S336
source: DYRK2 phosphorylates NDEL1 S336 to prime the phosphorylation of NDEL1 S332 by GSK3β.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A-B demonstrating DYRK2-induced phosphorylation of NDEL1 at S336, and by in silico analysis predicting S336 as a DYRK2 target site.

claim: GSK3β phosphorylates NDEL1 at S332
source: DYRK2 phosphorylates NDEL1 S336 to prime the phosphorylation of NDEL1 S332 by GSK3β.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 1A-B showing GSK3β-induced phosphorylation at S332, and by in silico analysis predicting S332 as a GSK3β target site.

claim: DYRK2 phosphorylation of NDEL1 S336 primes subsequent phosphorylation at S332 by GSK3β
source: DYRK2 phosphorylates NDEL1 S336 to prime the phosphorylation of NDEL1 S332 by GSK3β.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 1B showing that S336A mutation abolishes both S336 and S332 phosphorylation, while S332A mutation retains S336 phosphorylation.

claim: TARA scaffolds DYRK2 and GSK3β to form a tripartite complex
source: TARA, an interaction partner of NDEL1, scaffolds DYRK2 and GSK3β to form a tripartite complex and enhances NDEL1 S336/S332 phosphorylation.
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 4D-F showing protein-protein interactions among TARA, DYRK2, and GSK3β, and by data showing TARA overexpression enhances DYRK2-GSK3β interaction.

claim: TARA enhances NDEL1 S336/S332 phosphorylation
source: TARA, an interaction partner of NDEL1, scaffolds DYRK2 and GSK3β to form a tripartite complex and enhances NDEL1 S336/S332 phosphorylation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 4A-C showing TARA co-expression increases NDEL1 phosphorylation at S336 and S332.

claim: NDEL1 S336/S332 dual phosphorylation increases filamentous actin dynamics
source: This dual phosphorylation increases the filamentous actin dynamics.
evidence: The claim is supported by FRAP assay data in Figure 6B-F showing that NDEL1 phosphorylation affects F-actin dynamics in growth cone-like structures.

claim: NDEL1 S336/S332 phosphorylation enhances axonal outgrowth
source: Ultimately, the phosphorylation enhances both axonal and dendritic outgrowth and promotes their arborization.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 2 showing that NDEL1 phosphorylation increases axonal neurite length in cultured hippocampal neurons.

claim: NDEL1 S336/S332 phosphorylation enhances dendritic outgrowth
source: Ultimately, the phosphorylation enhances both axonal and dendritic outgrowth and promotes their arborization.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 2 showing that NDEL1 phosphorylation increases dendritic neurite length in cultured hippocampal neurons.

claim: NDEL1 S336/S332 phosphorylation promotes neuronal arborization
source: Ultimately, the phosphorylation enhances both axonal and dendritic outgrowth and promotes their arborization.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 3 showing that NDEL1 phosphorylation increases dendritic branching in layer II/III pyramidal neurons.

claim: DYRK2 was identified as a kinase responsible for NDEL1 phosphorylation through human kinome screening
source: Among the 218 serine/threonine kinases tested, we identified dual specificity tyrosine-phosphorylation-regulated kinase 2 (DYRK2) and homeodomain-interacting protein kinase 4 (HIPK4) as the candidates (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by the kinome screening data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 using band shift assay to detect NDEL1 phosphorylation.

claim: HIPK4 was identified as a kinase responsible for NDEL1 phosphorylation through human kinome screening
source: Among the 218 serine/threonine kinases tested, we identified dual specificity tyrosine-phosphorylation-regulated kinase 2 (DYRK2) and homeodomain-interacting protein kinase 4 (HIPK4) as the candidates (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by the kinome screening data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 using band shift assay to detect NDEL1 phosphorylation.

claim: 218 serine/threonine kinases were tested in the human kinome screening
source: Among the 218 serine/threonine kinases tested, we identified dual specificity tyrosine-phosphorylation-regulated kinase 2 (DYRK2) and homeodomain-interacting protein kinase 4 (HIPK4) as the candidates (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing the kinome screening methodology.

claim: DYRK2 and HIPK4 belong to the DYRK family
source: DYRK2 and HIPK4 belong to the DYRK family and share an evolutionarily conserved DYRK homology (DH)-box (Arai et al., 2007; Aranda et al., 2011; Becker et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Arai et al., 2007; Aranda et al., 2011; Becker et al., 1998).

claim: DYRK2 and HIPK4 share an evolutionarily conserved DYRK homology (DH)-box
source: DYRK2 and HIPK4 belong to the DYRK family and share an evolutionarily conserved DYRK homology (DH)-box (Arai et al., 2007; Aranda et al., 2011; Becker et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Arai et al., 2007; Aranda et al., 2011; Becker et al., 1998).

claim: DYRK family kinases often act as priming kinases for GSK3 on various targets
source: Moreover, DYRK family kinases often act as priming kinases for GSK3 on various targets (Cole et al., 2006; Nishi and Lin, 2005; Taira et al., 2012; Woods et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Cole et al., 2006; Nishi and Lin, 2005; Taira et al., 2012; Woods et al., 2001).

claim: DYRK2 induced significant phosphorylation of NDEL1
source: Indeed, DYRK2 induced significant phosphorylation of NDEL1 while co-expression of DYRK2 and GSK3βS9A, a constitutively active form of GSK3β, induced at least two phosphorylation bands (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A demonstrating NDEL1 phosphorylation by DYRK2.

claim: Co-expression of DYRK2 and GSK3βS9A induced at least two phosphorylation bands of NDEL1
source: Indeed, DYRK2 induced significant phosphorylation of NDEL1 while co-expression of DYRK2 and GSK3βS9A, a constitutively active form of GSK3β, induced at least two phosphorylation bands (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A demonstrating dual phosphorylation of NDEL1 by DYRK2 and GSK3β.

claim: GSK3βS9A is a constitutively active form of GSK3β
source: Indeed, DYRK2 induced significant phosphorylation of NDEL1 while co-expression of DYRK2 and GSK3βS9A, a constitutively active form of GSK3β, induced at least two phosphorylation bands (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about the S9A mutation in GSK3β.

claim: In silico analysis predicted NDEL1 S336 and S332 residues as target sites by DYRK2 and GSK3β, respectively
source: In silico analysis predicted NDEL1 S336 and S332 residues as the target sites by DYRK2 and GSK3β, respectively.
evidence: The claim is based on computational prediction methods applied to NDEL1 sequence.

claim: NDEL1S332A retained a single phosphorylation band by DYRK2 but lost GSK3β effect
source: When we tested each phospho-deficient mutant, S332A (NDEL1S332A) and S336A (NDEL1S336A), NDEL1S332A retained a single phosphorylation band by DYRK2, but lost GSK3β effect, while either NDEL1S336A or S332A/S336A double mutant (NDEL1S332/336A) showed no detectible phosphorylation band (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A showing phosphorylation patterns of NDEL1 mutants.

claim: NDEL1S336A showed no detectable phosphorylation band
source: When we tested each phospho-deficient mutant, S332A (NDEL1S332A) and S336A (NDEL1S336A), NDEL1S332A retained a single phosphorylation band by DYRK2, but lost GSK3β effect, while either NDEL1S336A or S332A/S336A double mutant (NDEL1S332/336A) showed no detectible phosphorylation band (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A showing phosphorylation patterns of NDEL1 mutants.

claim: NDEL1S332/336A double mutant showed no detectable phosphorylation band
source: When we tested each phospho-deficient mutant, S332A (NDEL1S332A) and S336A (NDEL1S336A), NDEL1S332A retained a single phosphorylation band by DYRK2, but lost GSK3β effect, while either NDEL1S336A or S332A/S336A double mutant (NDEL1S332/336A) showed no detectible phosphorylation band (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A showing phosphorylation patterns of NDEL1 mutants.

claim: Phosphorylation at NDEL1 S336 and S332 was identified from LC-MS/MS analysis of developing mouse brain lysates
source: We then assessed the PTMs of endogenous NDEL1 proteins isolated from postnatal day 7 (P7) developing mouse brain by LC-MS/MS analysis to see whether the S332 and 336 can be phosphorylated in vivo (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 3). Interestingly, among multiple PTMs identified, we observed masses indicating phosphorylation at NDEL1 S332 or S336 (Figure 1D), suggesting the potential roles of NDEL1 phosphorylation in neurodevelopmental processes.
evidence: The claim is supported by LC-MS/MS data shown in Figure 1C-D identifying phosphorylation at S332 or S336 in endogenous NDEL1 from mouse brain.

claim: NDEL1 S336/S332 phosphorylation peaked at embryonic day 18 (E18) and postnatal day 7 (P7) in developing mouse brain
source: In the brain lysates from various developmental stages, pNDEL1 signal peaked at embryonic day 18 (E18) and P7 (Figure 1E), the stage where residual neuronal migration and intense neurite outgrowth and maturation occur.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 1E showing pNDEL1 levels across developmental stages.

claim: E18 and P7 are stages where residual neuronal migration and intense neurite outgrowth and maturation occur
source: In the brain lysates from various developmental stages, pNDEL1 signal peaked at embryonic day 18 (E18) and P7 (Figure 1E), the stage where residual neuronal migration and intense neurite outgrowth and maturation occur.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about neurodevelopmental processes at these stages.

claim: Over-expression of DYRK2 and GSK3βS9A increased endogenous NDEL1 S336/S332 phosphorylation
source: Additionally, the increment of the endogenous NDEL1 phosphorylation by DYRK2-GSK3βS9A expression was detected by anti-pNDEL1 antibody (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 1F showing increased endogenous NDEL1 phosphorylation upon kinase overexpression.

claim: pNDEL1 signal in mouse brain slices was significantly diminished upon NDEL1 knockdown by in utero electroporation
source: The pNDEL1 signal in mouse brain slices was significantly diminished upon NDEL1 knockdown by in utero electroporation of an shRNA construct, further validating the immunostaining specificity of the antibody (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D showing reduced pNDEL1 signal upon NDEL1 knockdown.

claim: Significant pNDEL1 signal was detected in the growth cone of cultured primary hippocampal neurons
source: In cultured primary hippocampal neurons, the significant pNDEL1 signal was detected in the growth cone, a region of dynamic crosstalk between actin and microtubules (Figure 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data in Figure 1G showing pNDEL1 localization in growth cones.

claim: The growth cone is a region of dynamic crosstalk between actin and microtubules
source: In cultured primary hippocampal neurons, the significant pNDEL1 signal was detected in the growth cone, a region of dynamic crosstalk between actin and microtubules (Figure 1G).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about growth cone biology.

claim: pNDEL1 signal overlapped with phalloidin and α-tubulin in growth cones
source: This crosstalk is required for correct neurite extension and branching (Coles and Bradke, 2015; Pacheco and Gallo, 2016; Rodriguez et al., 2003). Moreover, the pNDEL1 signal overlapped with that of both phalloidin, a marker for F-actin, and α-tubulin.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data in Figure 1G showing colocalization of pNDEL1 with phalloidin and α-tubulin.

claim: Actin-microtubule crosstalk is required for correct neurite extension and branching
source: This crosstalk is required for correct neurite extension and branching (Coles and Bradke, 2015; Pacheco and Gallo, 2016; Rodriguez et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Coles and Bradke, 2015; Pacheco and Gallo, 2016; Rodriguez et al., 2003).

claim: Phosphorylated NDEL1 was prominently present in filopodia-like structures where both F-actin and microtubules are colocalized
source: Notably, phosphorylated NDEL1 was prominently present in filopodia-like structures where both F-actin and microtubules are colocalized (Figure 1G, arrowheads).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data in Figure 1G showing pNDEL1 localization in filopodia-like structures.

claim: NDEL1 knockdown significantly reduced total neurite length by about 31%
source: In cultured hippocampal neurons, NDEL1 knockdown significantly reduced both the total neurite length and the longest neurite length by about 31% and 33%, respectively (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 2A-C showing neurite length measurements in NDEL1 knockdown neurons.

claim: NDEL1 knockdown significantly reduced the longest neurite length by about 33%
source: In cultured hippocampal neurons, NDEL1 knockdown significantly reduced both the total neurite length and the longest neurite length by about 31% and 33%, respectively (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 2A-C showing neurite length measurements in NDEL1 knockdown neurons.

claim: Co-expression of shRNA-resistant NDEL1WT reversed neurite outgrowth defects caused by NDEL1 knockdown
source: Co-expression of an shRNA-resistant form of NDEL1WT, but not NDEL1S332/336A, effectively reversed these phenotypes providing specificity to the NDEL1 phosphorylation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 2A-C showing rescue of neurite outgrowth defects by NDEL1WT.

claim: Co-expression of shRNA-resistant NDEL1S332/336A did not reverse neurite outgrowth defects caused by NDEL1 knockdown
source: Co-expression of an shRNA-resistant form of NDEL1WT, but not NDEL1S332/336A, effectively reversed these phenotypes providing specificity to the NDEL1 phosphorylation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 2A-C showing failure of NDEL1S332/336A to rescue neurite outgrowth defects.

claim: Co-expression of DYRK2 and GSK3βS9A with NDEL1WT significantly increased total neurite length by about 22%
source: In addition, co-expression of DYRK2 and GSK3βS9A with NDEL1WT, but not with NDEL1S332/336A, significantly increased the total neurite length and the longest neurite length by about 22% and 19%, respectively (Figure 2D–F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 2D-F showing increased neurite length upon kinase overexpression with NDEL1WT.

claim: Co-expression of DYRK2 and GSK3βS9A with NDEL1WT significantly increased the longest neurite length by about 19%
source: In addition, co-expression of DYRK2 and GSK3βS9A with NDEL1WT, but not with NDEL1S332/336A, significantly increased the total neurite length and the longest neurite length by about 22% and 19%, respectively (Figure 2D–F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 2D-F showing increased neurite length upon kinase overexpression with NDEL1WT.

claim: Co-expression of DYRK2 and GSK3βS9A with NDEL1S332/336A did not significantly increase neurite length
source: In addition, co-expression of DYRK2 and GSK3βS9A with NDEL1WT, but not with NDEL1S332/336A, significantly increased the total neurite length and the longest neurite length by about 22% and 19%, respectively (Figure 2D–F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 2D-F showing no increase in neurite length upon kinase overexpression with NDEL1S332/336A.

claim: NDEL1 S332/336A knock-in resulted in diminished neurite lengths of primary cultured neurons
source: Furthermore, to avoid potential complications caused by an overexpression of NDEL1, we applied CRISPR/Cas9 based knock-in (KI) approach targeting mouse Ndel1 exon nine in order to generate a phospho-deficient NDEL1 S332/336A mutation with insertion of EGFP as the KI marker (Figure 2—figure supplement 2). NDEL1 S332/336A KI resulted in the diminished neurite lengths of the primary cultured neurons (Figure 2G–I, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 2G-I showing reduced neurite lengths in NDEL1 S332/336A knock-in neurons.

claim: NDEL1 phosphorylation at S336 and S332 up-regulates axon/dendrite outgrowth
source: Taken together, these results show that NDEL1 phosphorylation at S336 and S332 up-regulates axon/dendrite outgrowth.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple experimental results in Figure 2 showing effects of NDEL1 phosphorylation on neurite outgrowth.

claim: Suppression of NDEL1 expression in mouse brain decreases the number of dendritic branches
source: Suppression of NDEL1 expression in mouse brain decreases the number of dendritic branches (Saito et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature (Saito et al., 2017).

claim: Loss of NudE in Drosophila results in abnormal dendritic arborization
source: In Drosophila, the loss of NudE, a homolog of both NDE1 and NDEL1, results in abnormal dendritic arborization (Arthur et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature (Arthur et al., 2015).

claim: NDEL1 S336/S332 phosphorylation was prominently detected in neurons of cortical layers II/III in P14 mouse brain
source: NDEL1 S336/S332 phosphorylation was prominently detected in neurons of the cortical layers II/III in P14 mouse brain (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A showing pNDEL1 localization in cortical layers.

claim: NDEL1 knockdown decreased the number of intersections in Sholl analysis
source: NDEL1 knockdown decreased the number of intersections in Sholl analysis and the total length of dendrites (Figure 3A–C, Figure 3—video 1), in addition to the abnormal positioning of cortical neurons as previously reported (Figure 3A, arrowheads).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 3A-C showing Sholl analysis results in NDEL1 knockdown neurons.

claim: NDEL1 knockdown decreased the total length of dendrites
source: NDEL1 knockdown decreased the number of intersections in Sholl analysis and the total length of dendrites (Figure 3A–C, Figure 3—video 1), in addition to the abnormal positioning of cortical neurons as previously reported (Figure 3A, arrowheads).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 3A-C showing dendritic length measurements in NDEL1 knockdown neurons.

claim: NDEL1 knockdown caused abnormal positioning of cortical neurons
source: NDEL1 knockdown decreased the number of intersections in Sholl analysis and the total length of dendrites (Figure 3A–C, Figure 3—video 1), in addition to the abnormal positioning of cortical neurons as previously reported (Figure 3A, arrowheads).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 3A showing abnormal neuronal positioning, and by citation to previous reports.

claim: Co-expression of shRNA-resistant NDEL1WT reversed defects in dendritic arborization caused by NDEL1 knockdown
source: Co-expression of an shRNA-resistant form of NDEL1WT, but not NDEL1S332/336A, reversed this defect in dendritic arborization.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 3A-E showing rescue of dendritic arborization defects by NDEL1WT.

claim: Co-expression of shRNA-resistant NDEL1S332/336A did not reverse defects in dendritic arborization caused by NDEL1 knockdown
source: Co-expression of an shRNA-resistant form of NDEL1WT, but not NDEL1S332/336A, reversed this defect in dendritic arborization.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 3A-E showing failure of NDEL1S332/336A to rescue dendritic arborization defects.

claim: Suppression of NDEL1 phosphorylation decreased the total number of dendritic branches
source: The total number of dendritic branches decreased upon suppression of NDEL1 phosphorylation with no significant change in the longest dendritic branch length (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 3D showing decreased branch numbers in NDEL1 phosphorylation-deficient conditions.

claim: Suppression of NDEL1 phosphorylation had no significant effect on the longest dendritic branch length
source: The total number of dendritic branches decreased upon suppression of NDEL1 phosphorylation with no significant change in the longest dendritic branch length (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B showing no change in longest branch length.

claim: Suppression of NDEL1 phosphorylation resulted in decreased numbers of secondary and tertiary dendrites
source: In addition, suppression of NDEL1 phosphorylation resulted in decreased numbers of secondary and tertiary dendrites (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 3E showing decreased secondary and tertiary dendrite numbers.

claim: Over-expression of NDEL1WT and responsible kinases increased the total length of dendrites
source: Conversely, over-expression of NDEL1WT and responsible kinases increased the total length and the branching number of dendrites with more intersections in Sholl analysis (Figure 3F–J, Figure 3—figure supplement 1G–K, and Figure 3—video 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 3F-J showing increased dendritic length upon NDEL1WT and kinase overexpression.

claim: Over-expression of NDEL1WT and responsible kinases increased the branching number of dendrites
source: Conversely, over-expression of NDEL1WT and responsible kinases increased the total length and the branching number of dendrites with more intersections in Sholl analysis (Figure 3F–J, Figure 3—figure supplement 1G–K, and Figure 3—video 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 3F-J showing increased dendritic branching upon NDEL1WT and kinase overexpression.

claim: Over-expression of NDEL1WT and responsible kinases increased intersections in Sholl analysis
source: Conversely, over-expression of NDEL1WT and responsible kinases increased the total length and the branching number of dendrites with more intersections in Sholl analysis (Figure 3F–J, Figure 3—figure supplement 1G–K, and Figure 3—video 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 3F-J showing increased Sholl intersections upon NDEL1WT and kinase overexpression.

claim: NDE1 failed to effectively rescue neurite defects caused by NDEL1 knockdown
source: NDE1, a paralog of NDEL1 lacking C-terminal region harboring S336 and S332 residues, failed to effectively rescue neurite defects caused by NDEL1 KD (Figure 2—figure supplement 1L–O).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1L-O showing NDE1 cannot rescue NDEL1 knockdown phenotypes.

claim: NDE1 is a paralog of NDEL1 lacking C-terminal region harboring S336 and S332 residues
source: NDE1, a paralog of NDEL1 lacking C-terminal region harboring S336 and S332 residues, failed to effectively rescue neurite defects caused by NDEL1 KD (Figure 2—figure supplement 1L–O).
evidence: The claim is based on known structural differences between NDE1 and NDEL1.

claim: NDEL1 phosphorylation at S336 and S332 plays critical roles for neuronal arborization
source: Although in utero electroporation is intrinsically cell-type nonspecific and thus we cannot fully exclude the contribution of neuron-nonautonomous effects from neural or glial progenitors, these results collectively indicate that NDEL1 phosphorylation at S336 and S332 plays critical roles for neuronal arborization.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple experimental results in Figure 3 showing effects of NDEL1 phosphorylation on dendritic arborization.

claim: The interaction between NDEL1 and TARA has been identified previously
source: The interaction between NDEL1 and TARA has been identified previously (Hong et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature (Hong et al., 2016).

claim: TARA co-expression introduced at least two additional forms of NDEL1 bands distinct in size
source: Interestingly, TARA co-expression introduced at least two additional forms of NDEL1 bands distinct in size (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 4A showing NDEL1 band shifts upon TARA co-expression.

claim: Deletion of the NDEL1-interacting domain in TARA effectively blocked NDEL1 band shift
source: Moreover, deletion of the NDEL1-interacting domain, hTARAΔ413-499 (Hong et al., 2016) or mTARAΔ401-487, effectively blocked the band shift (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-B showing loss of NDEL1 band shift with TARA deletion mutants.

claim: Protein phosphatase treatment significantly diminished the mobility shifts of NDEL1 bands induced by TARA
source: To test whether the band mobility shifts are caused by PTMs, we treated protein phosphatase in vitro and it significantly diminished the mobility shifts of NDEL1 bands (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 4A showing phosphatase treatment reduces NDEL1 band shifts.

claim: TARA enhanced the signals detected by phosphoserine-specific antibody for NDEL1
source: In addition, TARA enhanced the signals detected by phosphoserine-specific antibody (anti-PhosphoSerine) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C showing increased phosphoserine signal upon TARA expression.

claim: The NDEL1-TARA interaction promotes NDEL1 phosphorylation
source: These results indicate that the NDEL1-TARA interaction promotes NDEL1 phosphorylation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing TARA-dependent NDEL1 phosphorylation.

claim: A phospho-peptide containing S336 residue was detected in LC-MS/MS analysis of NDEL1 co-expressed with TARA
source: To characterize the TARA-dependent NDEL1 phosphorylation, we utilized LC-MS/MS analysis of FLAG-NDEL1 proteins upon co-expression of NDEL1 and TARA in HEK293 cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 2). Among the multiple PTMs detected, a phospho-peptide containing S336 residue was present (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by LC-MS/MS data in Figure 4B showing phosphorylation at S336 in TARA-expressing cells.

claim: NDEL1S332A showed only a single phosphorylation band upon TARA co-expression
source: When we tested each single alanine mutant, NDEL1S332A and NDEL1S336A showed decreased TARA-dependent phosphorylation (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D). Particularly, NDEL1S332A showed only a single phosphorylation band, while NDEL1S336A showed a significant reduction in both phosphorylation bands.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 4C showing phosphorylation patterns of NDEL1 mutants with TARA.

claim: NDEL1S336A showed a significant reduction in both phosphorylation bands upon TARA co-expression
source: When we tested each single alanine mutant, NDEL1S332A and NDEL1S336A showed decreased TARA-dependent phosphorylation (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D). Particularly, NDEL1S332A showed only a single phosphorylation band, while NDEL1S336A showed a significant reduction in both phosphorylation bands.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 4C showing phosphorylation patterns of NDEL1 mutants with TARA.

claim: Endogenous TARA was co-immunoprecipitated with DYRK2
source: To assess how TARA increases NDEL1 phosphorylation by DYRK2-GSK3β kinases, we tested protein-protein interactions among TARA and the kinases. Endogenous TARA was co-IPed with both DYRK2 and GSK3β (Figure 4D–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 4D showing TARA-DYRK2 interaction.

claim: Endogenous TARA was co-immunoprecipitated with GSK3β
source: To assess how TARA increases NDEL1 phosphorylation by DYRK2-GSK3β kinases, we tested protein-protein interactions among TARA and the kinases. Endogenous TARA was co-IPed with both DYRK2 and GSK3β (Figure 4D–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 4E showing TARA-GSK3β interaction.

claim: Over-expression of TARA enhanced the interaction between DYRK2 and GSK3β
source: Furthermore, over-expression of TARA enhanced the interaction between DYRK2 and GSK3β, suggesting that TARA acts as a scaffold (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 4F showing increased DYRK2-GSK3β interaction upon TARA overexpression.

claim: TARA acts as a scaffold for DYRK2 and GSK3β
source: Furthermore, over-expression of TARA enhanced the interaction between DYRK2 and GSK3β, suggesting that TARA acts as a scaffold (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing TARA enhances DYRK2-GSK3β interaction.

claim: DYRK2, GSK3β, and TARA colocalized in mouse hippocampal neurons
source: Immunocytochemistry analysis confirmed their colocalization, further supporting their functional association (Figure 4G).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunocytochemistry data in Figure 4G showing colocalization of DYRK2, GSK3β, and TARA.

claim: Co-expression of NDEL1WT with TARA significantly increased total neurite length
source: In cultured neurons, the co-expression of NDEL1WT, but not NDEL1S332/336A, with TARA significantly increased both the total neurite length and the longest neurite length (Figure 5A–C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 5A-C showing increased neurite length upon NDEL1WT and TARA co-expression.

claim: Co-expression of NDEL1WT with TARA significantly increased the longest neurite length
source: In cultured neurons, the co-expression of NDEL1WT, but not NDEL1S332/336A, with TARA significantly increased both the total neurite length and the longest neurite length (Figure 5A–C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 5A-C showing increased neurite length upon NDEL1WT and TARA co-expression.

claim: Co-expression of NDEL1S332/336A with TARA did not significantly increase neurite length
source: In cultured neurons, the co-expression of NDEL1WT, but not NDEL1S332/336A, with TARA significantly increased both the total neurite length and the longest neurite length (Figure 5A–C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 5A-C showing no increase in neurite length upon NDEL1S332/336A and TARA co-expression.

claim: Co-expression of NDEL1WT and hTARAΔ413-499 did not increase total neurite length
source: On the other hand, co-expression of NDEL1WT and hTARAΔ413-499, which did not induce notable NDEL1 phosphorylation, did not increase the total neurite length and the longest neurite length (Figure 5D–F, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 5D-F showing no increase in neurite length with TARA deletion mutant.

claim: Co-expression of NDEL1WT and hTARAΔ413-499 did not increase the longest neurite length
source: On the other hand, co-expression of NDEL1WT and hTARAΔ413-499, which did not induce notable NDEL1 phosphorylation, did not increase the total neurite length and the longest neurite length (Figure 5D–F, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 5D-F showing no increase in neurite length with TARA deletion mutant.

claim: hTARAΔ413-499 did not induce notable NDEL1 phosphorylation
source: On the other hand, co-expression of NDEL1WT and hTARAΔ413-499, which did not induce notable NDEL1 phosphorylation, did not increase the total neurite length and the longest neurite length (Figure 5D–F, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing TARA deletion mutant does not induce NDEL1 phosphorylation.

claim: Only neurons expressing NDEL1WT with TARA had greater total dendrite length in P14 brain slices
source: Consistently, in P14 brain slices, only neurons expressing NDEL1WT with TARA had a greater total dendrite length and more branches dependently to the phosphorylation (Figure 5G–K, Figure 5—figure supplement 1E–I, and Figure 5—video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 5G-K showing increased dendritic length in neurons expressing NDEL1WT with TARA.

claim: Only neurons expressing NDEL1WT with TARA had more dendritic branches in P14 brain slices
source: Consistently, in P14 brain slices, only neurons expressing NDEL1WT with TARA had a greater total dendrite length and more branches dependently to the phosphorylation (Figure 5G–K, Figure 5—figure supplement 1E–I, and Figure 5—video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 5G-K showing increased dendritic branching in neurons expressing NDEL1WT with TARA.

claim: TARA recruits DYRK2 and GSK3β to induce NDEL1 S336/S332 phosphorylation, thereby enhancing neuronal morphogenesis
source: Thus, these results indicate that TARA recruits DYRK2 and GSK3β to induce NDEL1 S336/S332 phosphorylation, thereby enhancing neuronal morphogenesis.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple experimental results showing TARA-mediated NDEL1 phosphorylation and its effects on neuronal morphology.

claim: TARA directly binds to and stabilizes F-actin structure
source: TARA directly binds to and stabilizes the F-actin structure and it recruits NDEL1 toward F-actin (Hong et al., 2016; Seipel et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Hong et al., 2016; Seipel et al., 2001).

claim: TARA recruits NDEL1 toward F-actin
source: TARA directly binds to and stabilizes the F-actin structure and it recruits NDEL1 toward F-actin (Hong et al., 2016; Seipel et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Hong et al., 2016; Seipel et al., 2001).

claim: NDEL1 S336/S332 phosphorylation induced by TARA was detected in both insoluble F-actin fraction and soluble G-actin fraction
source: When we isolated F-actin from soluble G-actin via F-actin fractionation protocol, NDEL1 S336/S332 phosphorylation induced by TARA was detected in both insoluble F-actin fraction and soluble G-actin fraction, verifying that it can associate with F-actin structure (Figure 6A) comparable to its colocalization at growth cone (Figure 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by F-actin fractionation data in Figure 6A showing pNDEL1 in both fractions.

claim: NDEL1 knockdown suppressed fluorescence recovery in FRAP assay without changing half-maximum recovery time
source: NDEL1 knockdown suppressed the fluorescence recovery without changing the half-maximum recovery time (Figure 6B–F, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–D, and Figure 6—video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by FRAP assay data in Figure 6B-F showing reduced fluorescence recovery upon NDEL1 knockdown.

claim: Co-expression of shRNA-resistant NDEL1WT significantly rescued impaired F-actin dynamics caused by NDEL1 knockdown
source: Co-expression of an shRNA-resistant form of NDEL1WT, but not NDEL1S332/336A, significantly rescued the impaired F-actin dynamics indicating its phosphorylation dependency.
evidence: The claim is supported by FRAP assay data in Figure 6B-F showing rescue of F-actin dynamics by NDEL1WT.

claim: Co-expression of shRNA-resistant NDEL1S332/336A did not rescue impaired F-actin dynamics caused by NDEL1 knockdown
source: Co-expression of an shRNA-resistant form of NDEL1WT, but not NDEL1S332/336A, significantly rescued the impaired F-actin dynamics indicating its phosphorylation dependency.
evidence: The claim is supported by FRAP assay data in Figure 6B-F showing failure of NDEL1S332/336A to rescue F-actin dynamics.

claim: NDEL1 S336/S332 phosphorylation had minimal effect on insoluble F-actin fraction
source: Since NDEL1 S336/S332 phosphorylation had a minimal effect on an insoluble fraction of F-actin fraction, it is more likely that suppression of NDEL1 phosphorylation reduced F-actin formation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from F-actin fractionation data showing similar F-actin levels in pellet fractions.

claim: Suppression of NDEL1 phosphorylation reduced F-actin formation
source: Since NDEL1 S336/S332 phosphorylation had a minimal effect on an insoluble fraction of F-actin fraction, it is more likely that suppression of NDEL1 phosphorylation reduced F-actin formation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from FRAP assay data showing reduced fluorescence recovery upon NDEL1 phosphorylation suppression.

claim: Co-expression of either NDEL1WT or NDEL1S332/336A with NDEL1 shRNA enhanced microtubule dynamics
source: On the other hand, we tested microtubule dynamics by FRAP assay with mCherry-α-tubulin (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E–L). Co-expression of either NDEL1WT or NDEL1S332/336A with NDEL1 shRNA enhanced microtubule dynamics and the effect was not distinguishable.
evidence: The claim is supported by FRAP assay data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E-L showing enhanced microtubule dynamics with both NDEL1 forms.

claim: The effect of NDEL1WT and NDEL1S332/336A on microtubule dynamics was not distinguishable
source: On the other hand, we tested microtubule dynamics by FRAP assay with mCherry-α-tubulin (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E–L). Co-expression of either NDEL1WT or NDEL1S332/336A with NDEL1 shRNA enhanced microtubule dynamics and the effect was not distinguishable.
evidence: The claim is supported by FRAP assay data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E-L showing similar effects of NDEL1WT and NDEL1S332/336A on microtubule dynamics.

claim: NDEL1 regulates microtubule dynamics in collaboration with dynein-LIS1
source: While NDEL1 regulates microtubule dynamics in collaboration with dynein-LIS1 (Chansard et al., 2011; Niethammer et al., 2000; Yamada et al., 2010), interactions between NDEL1 and either dynein intermediate chain (DYNC1I1) or LIS1 was not significantly affected by the phosphorylations (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Chansard et al., 2011; Niethammer et al., 2000; Yamada et al., 2010).

claim: Interactions between NDEL1 and dynein intermediate chain (DYNC1I1) were not significantly affected by S336/S332 phosphorylations
source: While NDEL1 regulates microtubule dynamics in collaboration with dynein-LIS1 (Chansard et al., 2011; Niethammer et al., 2000; Yamada et al., 2010), interactions between NDEL1 and either dynein intermediate chain (DYNC1I1) or LIS1 was not significantly affected by the phosphorylations (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 6—figure supplement 2 showing similar NDEL1-DYNC1I1 interactions.

claim: Interactions between NDEL1 and LIS1 were not significantly affected by S336/S332 phosphorylations
source: While NDEL1 regulates microtubule dynamics in collaboration with dynein-LIS1 (Chansard et al., 2011; Niethammer et al., 2000; Yamada et al., 2010), interactions between NDEL1 and either dynein intermediate chain (DYNC1I1) or LIS1 was not significantly affected by the phosphorylations (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 6—figure supplement 2 showing similar NDEL1-LIS1 interactions.

claim: Both NDEL1WT and NDEL1S332/336A increased retrograde movement of GFP-LAMP1 labeled lysosomes
source: Furthermore, when we tested lysosomal trafficking in neurons as a readout for NDEL1-LIS1-dynein activity (Klinman and Holzbaur, 2015; Pandey and Smith, 2011), both NDEL1WT and NDEL1S332/336A increased a retrograde movement of GFP-LAMP1 labeled lysosomes (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by lysosomal trafficking data in Figure 6—figure supplement 3 showing increased retrograde movement with both NDEL1 forms.

claim: NDEL1 phosphorylation at S336 and S332 up-regulates F-actin dynamics at the growth cone of extending neurites
source: Taken together, our results indicate that NDEL1 phosphorylation at S336 and S332 up-regulates F-actin dynamics, at the growth cone of extending neurites, which is likely to underlie neuronal morphogenesis.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple experimental results showing NDEL1 phosphorylation effects on F-actin dynamics and neuronal morphology.

claim: NDEL1 plays multifaceted roles in neurodevelopmental processes
source: Nuclear distribution element-like 1 (NDEL1) plays multifaceted roles in neurodevelopmental processes (Chansard et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature (Chansard et al., 2011).

claim: NDEL1 expression in the nervous system begins at early embryonic stage and is maintained throughout adulthood
source: NDEL1 expression in the nervous system begins at early embryonic stage and is maintained throughout the adulthood (Pei et al., 2014; Sasaki et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Pei et al., 2014; Sasaki et al., 2000).

claim: Deficiency in Ndel1 results in embryonic lethality
source: Deficiency in Ndel1 results in embryonic lethality (Sasaki et al., 2005) and postmortem studies and human genetic studies have implicated NDEL1 in several neuropsychiatric diseases such as schizophrenia (Bradshaw and Hayashi, 2017; Burdick et al., 2008; Gadelha et al., 2016; Lipska et al., 2006; Nicodemus et al., 2010), both emphasizing the importance of NDEL1 functions in brain development.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature (Sasaki et al., 2005).

claim: NDEL1 has been implicated in schizophrenia
source: Deficiency in Ndel1 results in embryonic lethality (Sasaki et al., 2005) and postmortem studies and human genetic studies have implicated NDEL1 in several neuropsychiatric diseases such as schizophrenia (Bradshaw and Hayashi, 2017; Burdick et al., 2008; Gadelha et al., 2016; Lipska et al., 2006; Nicodemus et al., 2010), both emphasizing the importance of NDEL1 functions in brain development.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Bradshaw and Hayashi, 2017; Burdick et al., 2008; Gadelha et al., 2016; Lipska et al., 2006; Nicodemus et al., 2010).

claim: NDEL1 regulates neuronal precursor proliferation and differentiation in the developing brain
source: In the developing brain, NDEL1 regulates neuronal precursor proliferation and differentiation (Liang et al., 2007; Stehman et al., 2007; Ye et al., 2017), neuronal migration (Okamoto et al., 2015; Sasaki et al., 2005; Shu et al., 2004; Takitoh et al., 2012; Youn et al., 2009), and neuronal maturation (Hayashi et al., 2010; Jiang et al., 2016; Kamiya et al., 2006; Kuijpers et al., 2016; Saito et al., 2017; Shim et al., 2008; Youn et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Liang et al., 2007; Stehman et al., 2007; Ye et al., 2017).

claim: NDEL1 regulates neuronal migration in the developing brain
source: In the developing brain, NDEL1 regulates neuronal precursor proliferation and differentiation (Liang et al., 2007; Stehman et al., 2007; Ye et al., 2017), neuronal migration (Okamoto et al., 2015; Sasaki et al., 2005; Shu et al., 2004; Takitoh et al., 2012; Youn et al., 2009), and neuronal maturation (Hayashi et al., 2010; Jiang et al., 2016; Kamiya et al., 2006; Kuijpers et al., 2016; Saito et al., 2017; Shim et al., 2008; Youn et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Okamoto et al., 2015; Sasaki et al., 2005; Shu et al., 2004; Takitoh et al., 2012; Youn et al., 2009).

claim: NDEL1 regulates neuronal maturation in the developing brain
source: In the developing brain, NDEL1 regulates neuronal precursor proliferation and differentiation (Liang et al., 2007; Stehman et al., 2007; Ye et al., 2017), neuronal migration (Okamoto et al., 2015; Sasaki et al., 2005; Shu et al., 2004; Takitoh et al., 2012; Youn et al., 2009), and neuronal maturation (Hayashi et al., 2010; Jiang et al., 2016; Kamiya et al., 2006; Kuijpers et al., 2016; Saito et al., 2017; Shim et al., 2008; Youn et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Hayashi et al., 2010; Jiang et al., 2016; Kamiya et al., 2006; Kuijpers et al., 2016; Saito et al., 2017; Shim et al., 2008; Youn et al., 2009).

claim: NDEL1 functions are supposed to be regulated by multiple post-translational modifications
source: These functions are supposed to be regulated by multiple post-translational modifications (PTMs), but the detailed mechanism underlying them is yet fully understood.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from known NDEL1 functions and general knowledge about PTM regulation.

claim: NDEL1 directly binds to TARA
source: NDEL1 directly binds to Trio-associated repeat on actin (TARA, also known as TRIOBP isoform 1) (Hong et al., 2016), a short isoform of Trio-binding protein (TRIOBP) generated by alternative splicing (Riazuddin et al., 2006; Seipel et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature (Hong et al., 2016).

claim: TARA is a short isoform of TRIOBP generated by alternative splicing
source: NDEL1 directly binds to Trio-associated repeat on actin (TARA, also known as TRIOBP isoform 1) (Hong et al., 2016), a short isoform of Trio-binding protein (TRIOBP) generated by alternative splicing (Riazuddin et al., 2006; Seipel et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Riazuddin et al., 2006; Seipel et al., 2001).

claim: TARA associates with filamentous actin (F-actin)
source: TARA associates with filamentous actin (F-actin) and has functions in cell mitosis and cell migration (Hong et al., 2016; Seipel et al., 2001; Zhu et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Hong et al., 2016; Seipel et al., 2001; Zhu et al., 2012).

claim: TARA has functions in cell mitosis and cell migration
source: TARA associates with filamentous actin (F-actin) and has functions in cell mitosis and cell migration (Hong et al., 2016; Seipel et al., 2001; Zhu et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Hong et al., 2016; Seipel et al., 2001; Zhu et al., 2012).

claim: Abnormal aggregation of TARA has been observed in postmortem brains of patients with schizophrenia
source: Although its abnormal aggregation has also been observed in the postmortem brains of patients with schizophrenia (Bradshaw et al., 2014; Bradshaw et al., 2017), the role of the TARA in neurodevelopment remains largely unknown.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Bradshaw et al., 2014; Bradshaw et al., 2017).

claim: Perturbations of neuronal morphogenesis can cause severe deficits in brain functions in various neurodevelopmental disorders
source: Indeed, perturbations of this process can cause severe deficits in brain functions in various neurodevelopmental disorders such as autism spectrum disorder, attention deficit hyperactive disorder, and schizophrenia (Birnbaum and Weinberger, 2017; Forrest et al., 2018; Schubert et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Birnbaum and Weinberger, 2017; Forrest et al., 2018; Schubert et al., 2015).

claim: Orchestrated remodeling of the cytoskeleton is a crucial step for neuronal morphogenesis
source: Although its complex regulatory pathways composed of various players are still largely unknown, the orchestrated remodeling of the cytoskeleton is a crucial step for neuronal morphogenesis (Coles and Bradke, 2015; Dent and Gertler, 2003; Rodriguez et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Coles and Bradke, 2015; Dent and Gertler, 2003; Rodriguez et al., 2003).

claim: The C-terminal of NDEL1 (aa 191–345) contains multiple phosphorylation sites targeted by Aurora A and CDK1/CDK5
source: The C-terminal of NDEL1 (aa 191–345) contains multiple phosphorylation sites that are targeted by Aurora A and CDK1/CDK5 (Mori et al., 2007; Niethammer et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Mori et al., 2007; Niethammer et al., 2000).

claim: NDEL1 S336 and S332 phosphorylation sites are absent in NDE1
source: Interestingly, these TARA-DYRK2-GSK3β responsible sites, but not other phosphorylation sites, are absent in NDE1, a paralog of NDEL1 (Bradshaw et al., 2013; Mori et al., 2007; Niethammer et al., 2000; Shmueli et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Bradshaw et al., 2013; Mori et al., 2007; Niethammer et al., 2000; Shmueli et al., 2010).

claim: Suppression of DBZ enhances dual phosphorylation of NDEL1 at T219 and S251 by CDK5 and Aurora A
source: On the other hand, recently, Okamoto et al. determined that suppression of DISC1-binding zinc finger protein (DBZ) enhances the dual phosphorylation of NDEL1 at T219 and S251 by CDK5 and Aurora A, respectively (Okamoto et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature (Okamoto et al., 2015).

claim: Dual phosphorylation of NDEL1 at T219 and S251 inhibits LIS1-DISC1 transport to neurite tips
source: This dual phosphorylation inhibits LIS1-DISC1 transport to the neurite tips and thus microtubule elongation, thereby inhibiting radial migration of neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature (Okamoto et al., 2015).

claim: Phosphorylation by CDK5 alone enhances neuronal migration via increasing NDEL1 binding to katanin p60
source: Interestingly, phosphorylation by CDK5 alone enhances neuronal migration via increasing NDEL1 binding to katanin p60 (Toyo-Oka et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature (Toyo-Oka et al., 2005).

claim: Phosphorylation at S251 by Aurora A alone increases radial migration
source: Similarly, phosphorylation at S251 by Aurora A alone increases radial migration (Takitoh et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature (Takitoh et al., 2012).

claim: Dual phosphorylation of NDEL1 can have distinct effects to those elicited by single phosphorylation
source: These results indicate that dual phosphorylation of NDEL1 can have distinct effects to those elicited by single phosphorylation, and similar regulation may also exist regarding NDEL1 S336/S332 phosphorylation and TARA-DYRK2-GSK3β signaling.
evidence: The claim is inferred from comparison of effects of single versus dual phosphorylation at different NDEL1 sites.

claim: The actin-microtubule crosstalk is critical for neuronal morphogenesis
source: The actin-microtubule crosstalk is critical for neuronal morphogenesis (Coles and Bradke, 2015; Dong et al., 2015; Pacheco and Gallo, 2016; Rodriguez et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Coles and Bradke, 2015; Dong et al., 2015; Pacheco and Gallo, 2016; Rodriguez et al., 2003).

claim: NDEL1 regulates actin, microtubules, and intermediate filaments
source: TARA directly associates to F-actin (Seipel et al., 2001) while NDEL1 regulates actin, microtubules, and intermediate filaments (Hong et al., 2016; Nguyen et al., 2004; Niethammer et al., 2000; Shim et al., 2008; Toth et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Hong et al., 2016; Nguyen et al., 2004; Niethammer et al., 2000; Shim et al., 2008; Toth et al., 2014).

claim: TARA recruits NDEL1 toward the cell periphery and together they up-regulate local F-actin levels
source: We previously showed that TARA recruits NDEL1 toward the cell periphery and together they up-regulate local F-actin levels (Hong et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature (Hong et al., 2016).

claim: Some proteins involved in actin-microtubule crosstalk modulate F-actin dynamics while bound to microtubules
source: Some proteins involved in the actin-microtubule crosstalk, such as EB3, Drebrin, and CLIP-170, modulate F-actin dynamics while bound to microtubules (Jaworski et al., 2009; Lewkowicz et al., 2008; Mikati et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Jaworski et al., 2009; Lewkowicz et al., 2008; Mikati et al., 2013).

claim: NDEL1 may be associated with microtubule and simultaneously up-regulate F-actin dynamics, enhancing actin-microtubule crosstalk at growth cones
source: Likewise, we postulate that NDEL1 may be associated with microtubule and simultaneously up-regulate F-actin dynamics, enhancing actin-microtubule crosstalk at growth cones.
evidence: The claim is a speculation based on experimental observations and comparison to other proteins.

claim: The concerted action of DYRK2 and GSK3 on substrates has implicated these kinases in cell cycle, neurite outgrowth, neuronal migration, microtubule regulation, and apoptosis
source: The concerted action of DYRK2 and GSK3 on substrates, such as eIF2Bε, tau, CRMP4, DCX, c-Jun, and c-Myc (Cole et al., 2006; Nishi and Lin, 2005; Slepak et al., 2012; Taira et al., 2012; Tanaka et al., 2012; Weiss et al., 2013; Woods et al., 2001), has implicated these kinases in cell cycle, neurite outgrowth, neuronal migration, microtubule regulation, and apoptosis.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Cole et al., 2006; Nishi and Lin, 2005; Slepak et al., 2012; Taira et al., 2012; Tanaka et al., 2012; Weiss et al., 2013; Woods et al., 2001).

claim: TARA and CRMP1 have been identified in insoluble aggregates in brain samples of schizophrenia patients
source: Of particular note, TARA and CRMP1, another substrate of GSK3, have been identified in insoluble aggregates present in brain samples of schizophrenia patients (Bader et al., 2012), hinting at the potential involvement of TARA-DYRK2-GSK3β signaling module in the associated disease pathogenesis.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature (Bader et al., 2012).
